scenario: WIBTA if I forced my son to play sports or some other extracurricular? | I’ve been seriously contemplating forcing my 13 year old to play sports. Not because I want to force my dreams on him or something of the sort, but because he is incredibly LAZY to the point it internally frustrates me. He gets straight C’s in MIDDLE SCHOOL, gets in trouble for talking in class all the time, doesn’t clean up after himself ever (will literally eat his food and just leave it sitting there either downstairs or in his room for DAYS!!) , and generally speaking does absolutely nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn’t even shower unless told (will walk around the house with the same clothes on for a week during breaks). He’s one of those people that would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life, than leaving his comfort zone and being productive. Basically he doesn’t do anything he doesn’t want to do unless he absolutely has to. His mother, who I have shared visitation with, is in my opinion an absolutely terrible parent. She doesn’t push him to do anything. She just enables this sort of behavior by cleaning up after his messes, and barely punishing him for anything. I fear he’s shaping up to be a loser. I’ve been thinking of taking the initiative by forcing him to be apart of some team oriented extracurricular activity in order to snap these terrible bad habits, and complete lack of a work ethic. Something tells me being around friends of similar age all working really hard towards something and having fun in the process would give him the jolt he needs. My current thinking is telling him he has to play basketball for 1 season and if he doesn’t like it he can quit after the season is over. Would that make me an asshole? TL;DR: 13 year old son is lazy, so WIBTA if I forced him to play sports for a season to activate some sort of work ethic?

The parent is frustrated because the son gets straight C's in middle school, talks in class all the time, doesn't clean up after himself, and basically does nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn't even shower unless told, and walks around with the same clothes on for a week during breaks. The parent thinks the son would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life than leave his comfort zone and be productive. The son's mother, who shares visitation, is seen as a terrible parent because she doesn't push him to do anything and just enables his behavior by cleaning up after his messes and barely punishing him for anything. The parent is considering forcing the son to be part of a team-oriented extracurricular activity to snap out of these terrible bad habits and develop a work ethic. The parent's current thinking is to tell the son he has to play basketball for one season, and if he doesn't like it, he can quit after the season is over. The parent is wondering if that would make them an asshole. Alright, so first, I need to understand the situation fully. The parent is dealing with a 13-year-old son who is described as lazy, with poor academic performance, lack of personal hygiene, and a general lack of initiative. The parent is frustrated and worried that the son is shaping up to be a "loser" because of these habits. The parent's approach is to force the son into an extracurricular activity, specifically basketball, for one season, with the option to quit after that if he doesn't like it. Now, the question is whether this approach is right or wrong. To determine that, I need to consider several factors: the parent's intentions, the potential benefits and drawbacks of forcing the son into an activity, the son's feelings and autonomy, the role of the other parent, and the long-term implications of this decision. First, the parent's intentions seem to be good. They want to help the son develop a work ethic, improve his habits, and encourage him to be more productive. They recognize that the son's current behavior is problematic and could have negative consequences in the future. The parent is taking initiative to address these issues, which is commendable. However, the method of forcing the son into an activity raises some concerns. While the parent's intentions are good, forcing someone into an activity can lead to resentment, resistance, and a negative association with that activity. It could also undermine the son's sense of autonomy and self-efficacy, which are important for personal development. On the other hand, participating in team-oriented extracurricular activities can have numerous benefits for a child's development. It can teach teamwork, discipline, time management, and the importance of commitment. It can also provide a sense of accomplishment and belonging, which can boost self-esteem and motivation. But the key here is whether the son is willing to engage in these activities. If the son is forced into basketball, he might not put in the effort or derive any benefits from it. He might resist, which could lead to more conflict and frustration for both the parent and the son. Another consideration is the role of the other parent. The parent mentions that the son's mother is enabling the son's behavior by not pushing him and cleaning up after him. This lack of consistency between the parents could complicate the situation further. If one parent is trying to enforce structure and the other is not, it might send mixed signals to the son and make it harder for him to develop good habits. Additionally, the parent's approach of giving the son an option to quit after one season is a bit of a middle ground. It shows that the parent is willing to give the son some autonomy, but it's still a form of coercion. The son might feel pressured to comply with the parent's wishes, even if he doesn't want to participate in the activity. It's also important to consider the son's feelings and perspective. At 13 years old, he's at an age where he's developing his own identity and sense of self. Forcing him into an activity could make him feel like he's not in control of his own life, which could lead to resentment or rebellion. On the other hand, if the parent can find a way to involve the son in choosing the activity or at least discuss the reasons behind it, it might make the son more receptive to the idea. Moreover, the parent's approach might not address the root causes of the son's behavior. The son's laziness, poor academic performance, and lack of initiative could be symptoms of underlying issues, such as lack of motivation, low self-esteem, or even undiagnosed learning disabilities or mental health issues. Simply forcing him into an extracurricular activity might not address these deeper issues and could lead to further problems down the line. In addition, the parent's own frustration and the way they express it could impact the son's behavior. If the parent is constantly frustrated and communicates that frustration in a negative way, it could create a hostile environment that discourages the son from making positive changes. It's important for the parent to manage their own emotions and approach the situation in a constructive and supportive manner. Another aspect to consider is the potential for the son to develop a work ethic through other means. While extracurricular activities can be effective, there are other ways to instill a work ethic, such as household chores, part-time jobs, or even creative projects that the son is interested in. The key is to find activities that align with the son's interests and strengths, which can make him more motivated to participate and develop a work ethic. Furthermore, the parent's approach might not take into account the son's preferences and interests. If the son is forced into an activity he doesn't enjoy, it could lead to a negative experience and reinforce his resistance to trying new things. It's important for the parent to involve the son in the decision-making process and consider his input when choosing an extracurricular activity. Additionally, the parent's relationship with the son could be affected by this decision. If the parent is seen as controlling or overbearing, it might strain their relationship and make it harder for the son to open up and seek guidance in the future. Building a positive and supportive relationship is crucial for encouraging the son to make positive changes and develop a work ethic. In summary, while the parent's intentions are good and they are taking initiative to address their son's problematic behavior, forcing the son into an extracurricular activity without considering his feelings, preferences, and the underlying causes of his behavior could be counterproductive. It's important for the parent to approach the situation in a way that respects the son's autonomy, involves him in the decision-making process, and addresses the root causes of his behavior. Additionally, the parent should consider alternative approaches to instilling a work ethic and seek support from other resources, such as counseling or educational programs, if necessary.
